interactions.summary: Jiang introduces a thought experiment in which a daughter kills a beloved dog to test whether her parents love her more, using the setup to stage the impossible bind of punishment, forgiveness, and pedagogy.
Students try to solve the scenario, and one of them explicitly maps it onto Jesus by proposing self-punishment: the parent suffers personally so the child sees the wound she caused.

Jiang endorses the self-punishment answer and says that only by suffering personally can the parent both reveal love and stop future violence, which becomes his explanatory model for Jesus' sacrifice as reconciliation.
A student resists the metaphor as pathological and suggests therapy or education instead, opening the next packet's challenge to Jiang's forced either-or.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student objection with Jiang clarification request

claims.claim: Jiang's thought experiment makes the redemptive problem concrete by imagining a child who kills a dog to discover whether her parents love her more than the animal.
A student's proposed solution is that the parent punishes themselves so the child can see that the child's act wounded the parent more deeply and so understand forgiveness through self-suffering.
Jiang says the parent cannot simply do nothing or punish the child directly, because either response would fail to teach love correctly and could even intensify future violence.
Jiang argues that the only effective solution is for the parent to punish themselves, because that visible suffering convinces the child that she is loved and thereby reforms her desire.
Jiang says this parental self-punishment is the logic behind the sacrifice of Jesus: God shows true love through self-suffering so humans can return to loving God in reconciliation.
A student objects that the metaphor is strange and overly absolute, suggesting therapy as an alternative to Jiang's binary between punishment and permissiveness.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns original sin and redemption into a family melodrama where a daughter's cruelty is really a desperate test of whether love is real.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's shocking image and the hinge that lets Jiang translate abstract atonement theory into emotional pedagogy.

signature_moments.moment: The parent is trapped: punish the child and you prove love for the dog, forgive too easily and you teach nothing, so the parent absorbs the wound instead.
signature_moments.source_phrase: your only solution ... is you punish yourself
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This preserves Jiang's central causal chain for why sacrifice, not mere pardon, produces transformation.

signature_moments.moment: Jesus' sacrifice is framed as visible proof of divine love that teaches humans how to love God back.
signature_moments.source_phrase: that's the logic behind the sacrifice of Jesus
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's explicit doctrinal payoff and the bridge from metaphor to theology.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang uses reconciliation for the restored relationship in which God's self-sacrifice persuades humans to return to loving God.
Explained through the parent's self-punishment metaphor: divine suffering displays love and reforms the sinner's heart.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet leaves textual exposition for a vivid atonement thought experiment, then immediately draws student resistance that the model is too absolute and psychologically thin.
